{{Short description|American biologist (1932–2022)}}
'''Patricia Jackson DeCoursey''' (December 28, 1932 – January 1, 2022) was an American biologist. A leading researcher in the field of [[chronobiology]], her research focused on behavioral, physiological, and ecological aspects of mammalian [[circadian rhythms]].<ref name="about_the_authors">[http://www.sinauer.com/detail.php?id=1490#tents DeCoursey’s Textbook: Summary & About the Authors]</ref><ref name="SC_Faculty">{{cite web|title=Patricia J. DeCoursey SC Faculty Page|url=http://www.biol.sc.edu/DeCoursey|access-date=April 8, 2013}}</ref> She is credited with creating the first [[Phase response curve|Phase Response Curve]] (PRC).  PRC’s are used throughout the field today to help illustrate the change of a biological oscillation in response to an external stimulus.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Johnson|first=Carl|author2=Ken-ichi, Sato Honma|title=Phase Response Curves: What Can They Tell Us about Circadian Clocks ?|journal=Circadian Clocks from Cell to Human|year=1992|pages=209–249|url=http://as.vanderbilt.edu/johnsonlab/prcatlas/carltext/|access-date=April 8, 2013}}</ref>  She worked as a biology professor at the [[University of South Carolina]] (USC) from 1967 until her retirement as director of the [[W. Gordon Belser Arboretum]] in 2019.

==Biography==
At an early age, DeCoursey expressed much interest in nature. She became fascinated with the outdoors though traveling with her father, a physician, and the rest of her family to remote wilderness areas <ref>{{cite news|last=Monk|first=John|title=USC professor wins big environmental award|url=http://www.thestate.com/2012/04/27/2252461/the-belser-arboretum-is-open-to.html|access-date=25 April 2013|newspaper=The State|date=April 27, 2012}}</ref> While attending Hunter College High School in New York City she began collecting data on the [[songbirds]] of a hardwood forest in [[Long Island]]. She mapped the number and location of the birds as well as their distinctive calls. She entered this project in  the 1950 [[Intel Science Talent Search|Westinghouse Science Talent Search]] and was named a finalist along with her twin sister Cynthia (Jackson) Fisher.<ref name="scientific_america">{{cite news|last=Vanderkam|first=Laura|title=For Patricia DeCoursey, When It Comes to Biology, Timing Is Everything|url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/article.cfm?id=patricia-decoursey-biology-westinghouse|access-date=21 April 2013|newspaper=Scientificamerican|date=July 27, 2009}}</ref>

===Education===
DeCoursey's interest in ornithology led her to [[Cornell University]], where she received a degree in [[zoology]] in 1954.  She met George DeCoursey at Cornell University, where he was a student at the time. She married George DeCoursey in 1954. DeCoursey furthered her education at the [[University of Wisconsin, Madison]] where she earned a Ph.D. in zoology and [[biochemistry]].  She did postdoctoral research with [[Jürgen Aschoff]] at the [[Max Planck Institute for Behavioral Physiology|Max-Planck Institute for Behavioral Physiology]] in Erling-Andech, Germany for two years. She then continued her research at [[Washington State University]],<ref name="scientific_america"/>

===Career===
DeCoursey was a distinguished professor of biology at [[University of South Carolina]], researching mammalian circadian rhythms since she moved there with her husband in 1966.<ref name="SC_Faculty"/>

===Death===
DeCoursey died in [[Columbia, South Carolina]], on January 1, 2022, at the age of 89.<ref>{{cite web |title=Patricia Jackson DeCoursey |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/thestate/name/patricia-decoursey-obituary?id=32077874 |website=Legacy |access-date=28 January 2024}}</ref>

==Contributions to chronobiology==

===Phase Response Curve===
Decoursey is credited with the first published Phase Response Curve (PRC). The relevant paper was about flying squirrels kept in constant darkness and how they would respond to different pulses of light at different times of the day.  The compilation of this data produced the first PRC.<ref name="sciblogs">Zivkovic, Bora; aka "Coturnix" (2007). "Clock Tutorial #3c - Darwin On Time". A Blog Around the Clock. ScienceBlogs LLC)</ref>

===Mammalian Entrainment System===
DeCoursey was the first scientist to show that the mammalian clocks can be reset by light pulses. She also showed that the photoreceptive system responsible for [[entrainment (chronobiology)|entrainment]] is different from the system involved in visual image perception.<ref>{{cite journal|last=DeCoursey|first=Patricia|author2=Takahashi JS |author3=Bauman L |author4=Menaker M |title=Spectral sensitivity of a novel photoreceptive system mediating entrainment of mammalian circadian rhythms.|journal=Nature|date=Mar 8, 1984|volume=308|issue=5955|pages=186–8|pmid=6700721|doi=10.1038/308186a0|bibcode=1984Natur.308..186T |s2cid=4321911 }}</ref>

===Adaptive Value===
DeCoursey helped the scientific world understand the adaptive value of the mammalian biological clocks (found within the [[suprachiasmatic nucleus]] (SCN)). From April 1997-October 1998 she set up an enclosure for approximately 74 chipmunks. 30 chipmunks had lesions in their SCN, 24 others were surgical control and 20 others were intact controls. After 80 days she showed that the majority of the chipmunks killed by predators had lesions in their SCN. This gave evidence to support that having a mammalian circadian clock is a favorable trait that has been naturally selected for.<ref>{{cite journal|last=DeCoursey|first=Patricia|author2=Walker JK |author3=Smith SA. |title=A circadian pacemaker in free-living chipmunks: essential for survival?|journal=J Comp Physiol A|date=February 2000|volume=186|issue=2|pages=168–80|doi=10.1007/s003590050017|pmid=10707315}}</ref> 
In an outdoor enclosure, DeCoursey released white-tailed antelope ground squirrels which had various levels of SCN lesioned.  The squirrels displaying the most activity during the night had the highest amount of lesioning.<ref>{{cite journal|last=DeCoursey|first=Patricia|author2=Jill R Krulas |author3=Gary Mele |author4=Daniel C Holley |title=Circadian Performance of Suprachiasmatic Nuclei (SCN)-Lesioned Antelope Ground Squirrels in a Desert Enclosure|journal=Physiology & Behavior|date=November 1997|volume=62|issue=5|pages=1099–1108|doi=10.1016/S0031-9384(97)00263-1|pmid=9333206|s2cid=44970274 }}</ref>  This research has helped further our understanding of sleep related issues affecting humans such as [[jet lag]] or [[insomnia]].

===Later research===
Her later research focused on the physiological and behavioral aspects of [[circadian rhythms]]. She studied how the retina moves in response to the daily rhythm. Also, as mentioned above, her work on chipmunks helped uncover the adaptive value of the circadian clock in the wild. She has done experiments related to the adaptive value of clocks on antelope squirrels and golden-mantled squirrels. This research furthers our understanding of sleep-related issues affecting humans such as [[jet lag]] or [[insomnia]].<ref name="about_the_authors"/>

===Other achievements===
DeCoursey received the 2011 South Carolina Environmental Awareness Award for re-foresting the W. Gordon Belser Arboretum at the University of South Carolina, a ten-year initiative she led, as well as for various small gardens around the university. The arboretum is designated as an outdoor field classroom and laboratory for UofSC undergraduates, and it is also used for conducting a variety of educational outreach programs.<ref>{{cite news|title=USC professor wins 2011 Environmental Awareness Award|url=http://www.dnr.sc.gov/news/yr2012/april26/april26_awareness.html|access-date=13 April 2013|newspaper=Life's Better Outdoors: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources|date=26 April 2012}}</ref> According to an article in [[Scientific American]], DeCoursey "spends half her work time on the restoring the arboretum and organizing class visits, and the other half on her professorial duties."<ref name="scientific_america"/>

Decoursey was a member of the original Organizing Committees for both the [[Journal of Biological Rhythms]] and the [[Chronobiology#History|Society for Research on Biological Rhythms]] (SRBR). She was an active member on the Advisory Board for both groups and served two terms as SRBR’s Secretary.

DeCoursey was one of the activists who worked to create what is now the [[Congaree National Park]].
